दिल्ली-एनसीआर में अगले तीन दिनों तक भीषण गर्मी और हीट वेव का प्रकोप जारी रहने वाला है। भारतीय मौसम विभाग की ओर से जारी ताजा पूर्वानुमान के अनुसार 26 और 27 मई को पूरे एनसीआर क्षेत्र में येलो अलर्ट जारी किया गया है। इस दौरान अधिकतम तापमान 44 डिग्री सेल्सियस तक पहुंचने की संभावना जताई गई है, जबकि न्यूनतम तापमान 30 से 31 डिग्री सेल्सियस के आसपास बना रहेगा।
मौसम विभाग ने लोगों को दोपहर के समय विशेष सावधानी बरतने की सलाह दी है। मौसम विभाग के अनुसार, 26 मई को अधिकतम तापमान 44 डिग्री और न्यूनतम 30 डिग्री सेल्सियस दर्ज होने का अनुमान है। पूरे दिन हीट वेव की स्थिति बनी रहेगी।
विभाग ने चेतावनी जारी करते हुए कहा है कि दोपहर और शाम के समय तेज सतही हवाएं चलेंगी, जिससे गर्म हवाओं का असर और अधिक महसूस होगा। इसके अलावा 27 मई को भी मौसम लगभग इसी तरह बना रहेगा। अधिकतम तापमान 44 डिग्री और न्यूनतम 31 डिग्री सेल्सियस रहने की संभावना है।
मौसम विभाग ने इस दिन भी हीट वेव और तेज गर्म हवाओं का अलर्ट जारी किया है। दोपहर और शाम के समय तेज सतही हवाएं चल सकती हैं, जिससे लोगों को लू का खतरा बना रहेगा। लगातार बढ़ती गर्मी के चलते लोगों को घरों से बाहर निकलने में काफी परेशानी का सामना करना पड़ सकता है। हालांकि 28 मई से मौसम अचानक करवट लेने वाला है।
मौसम विभाग के अनुसार 28 मई को अधिकतम तापमान घटकर 43 डिग्री और न्यूनतम 32 डिग्री सेल्सियस तक पहुंच जाएगा। इस दिन गरज-चमक के साथ हल्की बारिश होने की संभावना जताई गई है। साथ ही 50 से 60 किलोमीटर प्रति घंटे की रफ्तार से तेज आंधी और तूफानी हवाएं चल सकती हैं। दोपहर और शाम दोनों समय हल्की बारिश और थंडर स्क्वॉल की चेतावनी जारी की गई है।
29 मई को मौसम में बड़ा बदलाव देखने को मिलेगा। अधिकतम तापमान में भारी गिरावट दर्ज की जाएगी और पारा करीब 36 डिग्री सेल्सियस तक पहुंच सकता है, जबकि न्यूनतम तापमान 28 डिग्री रहने का अनुमान है। इस दिन भी गरज-चमक के साथ हल्की बारिश, बिजली कड़कने, और 40 से 50 किलोमीटर प्रति घंटे की रफ्तार से तेज हवाएं चलने की संभावना है.
मौसम विभाग का कहना है कि बारिश और तेज हवाओं की वजह से लोगों को भीषण गर्मी से काफी राहत मिलेगी। 30 और 31 मई को भी मौसम सुहावना बने रहने की संभावना है। इन दोनों दिनों में अधिकतम तापमान 35 से 36 डिग्री और न्यूनतम तापमान 25 डिग्री सेल्सियस के आसपास रहेगा।
मौसम विभाग ने इन दिनों के लिए ‘नो वार्निंग’ जारी की है, हालांकि गरज के साथ हल्की बारिश की संभावना बनी रहेगी। आर्द्रता का स्तर 70 से 40 प्रतिशत तक रह सकता है।
मौसम विशेषज्ञों के मुताबिक पश्चिमी विक्षोभ और बदलते मौसमी सिस्टम के प्रभाव से एनसीआर के मौसम में यह बड़ा बदलाव देखने को मिलेगा। फिलहाल लोगों को अगले दो से तीन दिनों तक भीषण गर्मी और लू से सावधान रहने की जरूरत है, जबकि 29 मई के बाद मौसम राहत देने वाला साबित हो सकता है।
(इनपुट-आईएएनएस)

उमस भरी गर्मी के बाद एक बार फिर लोगों को राहत मिलने की उम्मीद है। मौसम विभाग ने देश के अधिकांश हिस्सों में एक बार फिर बारिश को लेकर अलर्ट जारी किया है। मौसम विभाग ने बिहार और ओडिशा में आज मूसलाधार बारिश का अलर्ट जारी किया है। अरुणाचल प्रदेश, छत्तीसगढ़, झारखंड, नागालैंड, मणिपुर, मिजोरम, त्रिपुरा, पश्चिम बंगाल, सिक्किम, असम और मेघालय में भी आज तेज वर्षा हो सकती है। अंडमान और निकोबार द्वीप समूह, आंध्र प्रदेश, जम्मू-कश्मीर, लद्दाख, बिहार, पश्चिम बंगाल के गांगेय क्षेत्र, झारखंड, सिक्किम, कर्नाटक और ओडिशा में तूफान की आशंका है।
असम के कई जिलों में बाढ़ की स्थिति बनी हुई है। मौसम विभाग ने आज और सोमवार को राज्य के कई जिलों में तेज बारिश का अनुमान व्यक्त किया है।असम राज्य आपदा प्रबंधन प्राधिकरण के अनुसार छह जिले शिवसागर, लखीमपुर, दरांग, सोनितपुर, धेमाजी और जोरहाट बाढ़ से प्रभावित हैं। गुवाहाटी और शिवसागर के कई इलाकों में जलभराव और बाढ़ के कारण वाहनों का आवागमन बाधित हो गया है।
वहीं दिल्ली-एनसीआर के लोगों के लिए इस सप्ताह मौसम राहत भरा रहने की उम्मीद है। भारत मौसम विज्ञान विभाग (आईएमडी) के ताजा पूर्वानुमान के अनुसार 14 जुलाई से 19 जुलाई तक पूरे सप्ताह आसमान में आंशिक रूप से बादल छाए रहेंगे। इस दौरान कहीं भी किसी तरह की मौसम संबंधी चेतावनी जारी नहीं की गई है। यानी फिलहाल भारी बारिश, लू, आंधी या अन्य किसी गंभीर मौसमीय गतिविधि की संभावना नहीं जता ई गई है।
मौसम विभाग के अनुसार, पूरे सप्ताह दिन का अधिकतम तापमान लगभग 38 डिग्री सेल्सियस के आसपास बना रहेगा, जबकि न्यूनतम तापमान 27 से 29 डिग्री सेल्सियस के बीच रहने का अनुमान है। बादलों की लगातार आवाजाही के कारण तेज धूप का असर कुछ कम हो सकता है। इसके साथ ही हल्की बारिश और बीच-बीच में चलने वाली तेज हवाएं लोगों को उमस और बढ़ती गर्मी से राहत दे सकती हैं।
14 जुलाई को अधिकतम तापमान 38 डिग्री और न्यूनतम 27 डिग्री सेल्सियस रहने का अनुमान है। मौसम का पूर्वानुमान आंशिक रूप से बादल छाए रहने का है और किसी प्रकार की चेतावनी जारी नहीं की गई है। 15 जुलाई को भी मौसम लगभग समान रहेगा। अधिकतम तापमान 38 डिग्री और न्यूनतम 28 डिग्री सेल्सियस रहने की संभावना है। इस दिन भी आसमान में आंशिक बादल छाए रहेंगे।
16 जुलाई को अधिकतम तापमान 38 डिग्री तथा न्यूनतम 27 डिग्री सेल्सियस रहने का पूर्वानुमान है। मौसम विभाग ने इस दिन भी पार्टली क्लाउडी स्काई यानी आंशिक रूप से बादल छाए रहने की बात कही है। 17 जुलाई को अधिकतम तापमान 38 डिग्री और न्यूनतम 29 डिग्री सेल्सियस रह सकता है। 18 जुलाई को अधिकतम तापमान 38 डिग्री और न्यूनतम 29 डिग्री सेल्सियस रहेगा। बादलों की आवाजाही जारी रहेगी और मौसम सामान्य बना रहेगा। 19 जुलाई को भी मौसम में कोई बड़ा बदलाव देखने को नहीं मिलेगा। अधिकतम तापमान 38 डिग्री और न्यूनतम 29 डिग्री सेल्सियस रहने का अनुमान है।
इस पूरे सप्ताह एनसीआर में मौसम सामान्य रहने की संभावना है। हालांकि दिन का तापमान 38 डिग्री के आसपास बना रहेगा, लेकिन बादलों की आवाजाही, हल्की बारिश और तेज हवाओं के कारण लोगों को भीषण गर्मी से कुछ राहत मिलने की उम्मीद है। मौसम विभाग ने फिलहाल किसी भी प्रकार की गंभीर मौसमीय स्थिति की आशंका नहीं जताई है, जिससे आम जनजीवन सामान्य रहने की संभावना है।

मेरठ में शुक्रवार सुबह मौसम साफ रहा और तेज धूप निकली। इससे गर्मी और उमस बढ़ गई। सुबह से ही लोगों को परेशानी का सामना करना पड़ा। गुरुवार सुबह हुई बारिश के बाद दिन में फिर गर्मी और उमस बढ़ गई थी। बारिश के बावजूद तापमान में ज्यादा गिरावट नहीं हुई।
मौसम विभाग के अनुसार, शुक्रवार को मेरठ में बारिश की संभावना नहीं है। अधिकतम तापमान करीब 34 डिग्री और न्यूनतम तापमान 24 डिग्री सेल्सियस के आसपास रह सकता है। सुबह मौसम सुहाना रहेगा, लेकिन धूप निकलने के बाद गर्मी और उमस बढ़ने की संभावना है।
बीते दिनों हुई बारिश से वातावरण में नमी बनी हुई है। इसी वजह से तापमान सामान्य से कम होने के बावजूद उमस ज्यादा महसूस हो रही है। मौसम वैज्ञानिक डॉ. यूपी शाही के अनुसार, बारिश नहीं होने और धूप निकलने से हवा में प्रदूषक तत्वों का असर बढ़ सकता है। मेरठ का AQI करीब 150 दर्ज किया गया है, जो खराब श्रेणी में है।
मौसम बदलने से अस्पतालों में बढ़े मरीज
लगातार बदल रहे मौसम का असर लोगों की सेहत पर भी पड़ रहा है। अस्पतालों में मरीजों की संख्या बढ़ रही है। वायरल इंफेक्शन और एलर्जी से जुड़ी शिकायतों वाले मरीज ज्यादा पहुंच रहे हैं। मौसम साफ रहने से शहर में जलभराव वाले स्थानों पर राहत मिलने की उम्मीद है। हालांकि, दोपहर में तेज धूप और वातावरण में नमी के कारण गर्मी और उमस का असर बना रह सकता है।

Taiwan could see an additional 53 days a year of extreme heat — when temperatures reach 36°C or higher — by the end of this century, Central Weather Administration specialist Chang Wan-yu (張琬玉) said yesterday.
The estimate was based on 100 years of data, which showed that average temperatures have risen by 1.5°C and summers have become longer, she said.
Under the most severe global warming estimates, temperatures could rise by a further 3.4°C by the end of the century, meaning Taiwan could see nearly two additional months per year of extreme heat, she added.
Photo: Liao Chen-huei, Taipei Times
In 2020, the Taipei weather station recorded 46 days in which temperatures surpassed 36°C, she said.
Global warming is directly impacting Taiwan’s weather systems, as the first day of temperatures dipping below 14°C and the first autumn front have steadily arrived later in the year, Chang said.
Rising temperatures also affect rainfall, with years of low rainfall becoming more frequent between 1960 and 2020, compared with before 1960, she said.
From 1990 to 2015, the maximum daily precipitation per year has become more extreme, she added.
The Oceanic Nino Index, a metric for tracking the El Nino phenomenon, has continued to rise from negative values at the start of this year to 1.8 between May and July, she said.
From June 2023 to June 2024, global temperatures rose to unprecedented levels for 13 consecutive months, with 2024 marking the hottest year since records began in 1850, Chang said.
Estimates for global temperature increases range from 1.5°C to 2°C, but a small discrepancy of 0.5°C could have a significant impact on the global climate, as it could raise the proportion of coral reefs experiencing bleaching from 70 percent to 99 percent, she said.
The extra 0.5°C could also mean that the proportion of the population exposed to extreme heat once every five years would rise from 14 percent to 37 percent, she added.
Compound climate events — such as droughts and heat waves occurring simultaneously or consecutively — could amplify their impacts, Chang said.
Meteorological droughts are poised to become more severe, frequent and widespread, while typhoons are expected to become more intense, but less frequent, she added.

Lisa Sueyres told the Santa Barbara Unified School Board on Tuesday that her classroom hit 91.9 degrees during last week’s historic heat wave, even with two fans at full blast.
Sueyres, a performing arts teacher at La Colina Junior High School, said that students and staff are suffering and urged the board to pursue a “heat emergency” plan.
She joins a long line of teachers advocating for the same thing. And thanks to a last-minute extension to a state grant program, the district may be able to complete some air conditioning upgrades that previously hung in the balance, but teachers want to see a plan now.
Last week, Sueyres’s classroom did not dip below 85 degrees, she added. Yet no minimum day was implemented, as it was for an extreme heat forecast in August. Even then, La Colina was not included among the six schools placed on a minimum day schedule.
Only two spaces at La Colina have air conditioning, she claimed. “The district needs a concrete and equitable plan with what we have now” for cooling down campuses, she said, which includes protecting employees as well as students.
“It is not new information that temperatures continue to rise globally,” she said. “We need a plan for access to cooling spaces on all campuses.”
Teacher Kat Ross said teachers have “witnessed firsthand the effects of climate change on students in our district,” made worse by older buildings without proper ventilation, let alone air conditioning. Some classrooms reached 100 degrees last week, Ross said, and students experienced heat stress, sweating, lethargy, and difficulty concentrating.
“We need to be prepared,” Ross said. “This means having a heat response plan for temperatures inside classrooms, not just outside temperatures.”
District spokesperson Ed Zuchelli explained that because Santa Barbara’s climate has historically been mild, many schools were built without air conditioning — and old infrastructure is costly and challenging to upgrade. The older the school, the more expensive it will be because of potential issues, including the need to install ducting and test for asbestos and lead.
On the district’s end, it is not entirely for lack of trying. It has upgraded a few schools’ HVAC (heating, ventilation, and air conditioning) systems, established protocols for days with extreme heat, tinted classroom windows, and provided teachers with fans, Zuchelli has said.
It also went through the slow, complex process of applying for a state grant in 2023 to assess and replace its HVAC systems in five additional schools, said Steve Venz, the district’s chief operating officer, at Tuesday’s meeting. He explained that the grant covers up to 50 percent of the costs, while the district’s capital improvement funds would cover the remainder.
Despite pushback from legislators, applications for that grant — called CalSHAPE — closed abruptly in 2024, making $191 million in unused funds inaccessible to school districts. On August 31, the program officially sunsetted, and the remaining funds will return to utility companies, which claim they will use them to reimburse ratepayers.
At the last minute, however, legislators passed a budget trailer bill to give districts that already received the funding, such as Santa Barbara Unified, three additional years to finish projects before the state takes the money back. If this had not passed, the district would have had to give back the $6 million in funding it received, including the $700,000 already spent.
But now it can finish what it started.
Venz said the grant allowed the district to begin constructing and replacing HVAC systems at four elementary schools — Cleveland, Franklin, Harding, and Santa Barbara Community Academy — and Santa Barbara Jr. High School. These are schools with some of the district’s youngest and most socioeconomically disadvantaged students.
Those projects are on hold while the district awaits confirmation from the California Energy Commission to proceed under the grant extension.
“But we still … we’re also part of 221 school districts that are waiting for that confirmation as well,” he said.
Needless to say, it will take a while. Still, teachers want action now.
“For accountability and transparency, we need to know the plan,” Ross said, calling for a transparent, accountable timeline for installing A/C at all schools. “Let’s get this fixed so our students can perform at their best.”

South Korea Producer Prices Rebound in August as Heat Wave Sends Spinach Soaring 52%
South Korea's producer prices rebounded in August after just one month of decline, driven by surging agricultural and livestock prices caused by the heat wave and rising energy costs. According to the "August 2026 Producer Price Index (preliminary)" released by the Bank of Korea on the 18th, the index stood at 129.64 (2020=100), up 0.2% from July. In July, the index had fallen 0.4% due to declining international oil prices—its first drop in 11 months—but it returned to an upward trajectory within a month. Compared with the same month a year earlier, the index rose 7.9%, a wider gain than July's 7.7%.
The biggest driver of the rebound was agricultural, forestry and marine products. The category climbed 3.8% month-over-month, with agricultural products jumping 4.9% on poor harvests caused by the heat wave, and livestock products rising 2.8% on reduced supply from livestock deaths. Marine products edged up just 0.1%. Among individual items, spinach posted the steepest increase at 51.9% over the month, followed by pork at 5.4% and other fish at 7.3%. As a result, food products rose 1.8% and fresh food items climbed 7.4%. Notably, producer prices excluding food products remained flat from the previous month, indicating that the increase was effectively concentrated in food prices.
The energy sector added further upward pressure. Electricity, gas, water and waste rose 0.9%, largely due to an 11.0% surge in industrial city gas as higher international oil prices fed through with a lag. Coal and petroleum products also rose 0.4%, with solvents up 3.7% and jet fuel up 6.1%. Overall manufactured goods were unchanged from the previous month, as gains in coal and petroleum products were offset by a 0.7% decline in electrical equipment. Within manufactured goods, food-related items stood out, with cola up 4.6% and canned tuna up 9.5%.
The services sector was flat. Restaurant and accommodation services rose 0.6%, but financial and insurance services fell 1.5% as brokerage commissions declined amid the downturn in the South Korean stock market, dragging down the overall figure. Wiring harnesses fell 8.8%, one of the steepest declines among individual items this month.
Unlike producer prices, the Domestic Supply Price Index declined. The August index fell 1.3% from the previous month, extending its decline to two consecutive months. Raw materials fell 4.6%, intermediate goods 1.0%, and final goods 0.9%, with the declines concentrated in imports. The drop reflected the July decline in Dubai crude prices, customs clearance lags, and a 6.1% month-over-month fall in the exchange rate. The Total Output Price Index, which includes domestic shipments and exports, also fell 1.2%, mainly due to a 2.0% decline in manufactured goods on lower export prices.
The outlook for September suggests upward pressure will intensify further. The resumption of conflict in the Middle East has sent international oil prices sharply higher, and industrial city gas rates have been raised again. Lee Heung-hoo, head of the Bank of Korea's price statistics team, said, "The resumption of conflict in the Middle East has caused international oil prices to rise sharply, and wholesale industrial city gas rates were also raised in September." He added, "These factors are expected to act as upside pressures on producer prices." He further explained, "Through the 16th of this month, average international oil prices have risen 29% compared with August, and September industrial city gas rates have increased by 6.6%."
Producer prices had risen for nine consecutive months starting in September of last year, before flattening in June, declining in July, and rebounding in August. Given that this rebound resulted from a temporary supply shock—the heat wave—combined with rising energy prices rather than demand-side factors, weather conditions and the Middle East situation are expected to be the key variables shaping the trajectory of prices going forward.

Protein quality changes when food is exposed to extreme heat
Severe heating changed soy protein, reduced amino acid availability in mice, and altered one social response after feeding.
Food processing does more than change taste and texture. In some shelf-stable foods, very high temperatures are used to kill microbes so the products can be stored safely for longer periods.
But intense heat can also change the food itself.
A new mouse experiment suggests that very high heat can make soy protein harder to digest. As a result, the body may absorb fewer amino acids from the protein.
High heat changes protein quality
Proteins are broken down during digestion into amino acids, smaller building blocks that the body can absorb.
If processing changes the protein too much, digestive enzymes may have a harder time breaking it apart.
Dr. Tomoko T. Asai of Kyoto University wanted to understand what happens to proteins after they go through intense food processing.
“What happens to food-derived molecules after we eat them?” Dr. Asai said.
“I wanted to know whether food processing changes these proteins’ absorption as well as their biological effects.”
The team focused on soy protein isolate, a concentrated soy ingredient that is mostly protein.
They mixed it with water and heated it to 250°F (121°C) for 20 minutes, conditions designed to resemble the high-temperature sterilization used for some packaged foods.
Heating reduces recoverable amino acids
After heating, the soy still contained almost the same amount of nitrogen, which researchers commonly use to estimate total protein.
Yet the amount of amino acids they could recover from that protein dropped by about 10%.
That difference is important because most of the protein had not simply disappeared.
Instead, the heat appears to have chemically changed some of its amino acids and protein structures.
Heat changes protein chemistry
Laboratory tests showed that the heated proteins had been altered in several ways.
The researchers also found changes in certain sugars and ammonia, signs that several heat-driven chemical reactions may have taken place.
However, the team did not identify exactly which new compounds formed. That means the researchers know the protein changed, but they cannot yet say which specific chemical changes mattered most.
Digestion became more difficult
The next step was to see whether digestive enzymes could still break down the heated soy protein.
The researchers exposed heated and unheated soy to enzymes that perform major parts of protein digestion.
The unheated soy became completely soluble. In contrast, every gram of heated soy protein isolate left about 53 milligrams of insoluble material behind, and that material still contained protein.
Protein fragments resist digestion
The heated soy also produced more small protein fragments that resisted further breakdown by additional enzymes.
Some amino acids were therefore still present, but they remained inside material that was more difficult for digestive enzymes to take apart.
This matters because protein is useful nutritionally only when digestion can make its amino acids available. Simply measuring how much protein is present does not necessarily show how easily that protein can be used.
Mice had fewer amino acids
The team then tested what happened inside the body. Twelve-week-old male mice received a single dose of either heated or unheated soy protein after an 18-hour fast.
Blood was collected 30, 60, and 120 minutes later. This part of the experiment was small, with only four mice for each treatment at each time point.
Several amino acids were lower in the blood of mice given heated soy. By 120 minutes, the total amount of free amino acids in their blood was also lower than in mice given the unheated protein.
These results suggest that severe heating reduced how much of the soy’s amino acids became available in the bloodstream.
The experiment could not determine whether poorer digestion, reduced absorption, changes after absorption, or a combination of these processes produced the difference.
One social behavior changed
The researchers also wanted to know whether longer exposure could affect the mice in other ways.
Young male mice ate diets containing either heated or unheated soy protein for six weeks, with soy serving as their only protein source.
Both groups gained weight at a similar rate. The researchers also found no clear differences in tests designed to measure anxiety-like behavior or the ability to recognize a new object.
A difference appeared when the mice were tested with other mice. Both groups preferred being near another mouse rather than an empty cage, suggesting that their basic interest in social contact remained similar.
The researchers then introduced a second, unfamiliar mouse. Mice fed unheated soy preferred the new stranger, while mice fed the heated soy did not show the same preference.
Serotonin offered a clue
The team also measured serotonin, a chemical messenger involved in communication within the body. Peripheral serotonin, meaning serotonin outside the brain, is produced by specialized cells in the gut.
Mice that ate the heated soy had blood serotonin levels at roughly half those of the comparison group. However, their fasting levels of tryptophan, an amino acid used to make serotonin, remained similar.
Serotonin measured across the whole brain also did not differ between the groups. The researchers therefore did not find evidence of a general drop in brain serotonin.
They suggested that heat-altered protein fragments, or substances produced from them by gut microbes, could affect serotonin production in the gut.
The team did not directly measure gut microbes, serotonin-producing gut cells, or individual parts of the brain, so this possible explanation remains unproven.
“Clearly, the same amount of protein does not always mean the same nutritional availability,” said Dr. Asai.
What this means
The findings do not mean that cooked soy is harmful or that processed foods change human social behavior. The experiment involved only male mice, one type of soy protein isolate, and one severe heating condition.
Some parts of the work also involved very small numbers of animals.
The researchers could not tell whether the behavioral difference came from reduced amino acid availability, newly formed compounds in the heated protein, or another effect of the treatment.
What the results do show is that intense food processing can change more than the amount of protein measured in a product.
Under these specific conditions, severe moist heating made soy protein harder to digest, reduced amino acid availability in mice, and was linked with a narrow change in how the animals responded to an unfamiliar mouse.
More work is needed to identify the altered protein compounds and determine whether similar effects occur under other food-processing conditions or in humans.
The study is published in the journal npj Science of Food.

NEWBURGH, Ind. (WFIE) - It’s been all hands on deck at A+Derr.
The heat is leading to higher than average repairs and replacements to broken AC units, and the company’s service department working nearly nonstop.
Sales manager Jake Tison says many calls are emergencies with the heat index in the triple digits.
“It’s been crazy temperatures, well over 100 degree heat index, lots of customers. It can be upwards of 80 or 90 degrees in some of these houses which is a concern,“ Tison stated.
Managers say there are some myths surrounding AC in the heat.
One is, contrary to popular belief, changing the temperature when you’re not at home can actually make the unit run harder, risking damage rather than saving money.
They also say modern units don’t naturally lose their refrigeration, like Freon, and say if something is wrong, something is usually broken.
“A lot of times what we find is a lot of it’s due to improper maintenance on a system, so when we get to the job, it hasn’t been cleaned in three years and it pops a capacitor or fan motor, a lot of normal things that do fail over the years with this equipment,“ Tison stated.
They say some jobs are simple like replacing a filter, but if the job is more intensive, they say not do it on your own. They say you could risk further damage or even injury.
“Feel free to call. We’re staffed 24/7 to be able to take care of people’s needs and the do-it-yourselfers on YouTube turns out bad a lot of times so let the professionals take care of this stuff,” Tison stated.
Officials say with next week’s temperatures much cooler, it would be a great time to have your unit checked in case temperatures go up again.

BBC Weather said Spain's national weather agency, AEMET, warned of heavy rain in the country's east and issued a red alert for Barcelona's coastline. The flooding and heavy rainfall left one person dead, and authorities urged people to avoid any unnecessary travel.
Footage shared on Instagram showed rescue crews responding, cars sitting partly underwater, and floodwater entering a metro station.
Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez warned of "very complicated situations" as the storm moved through the area.
More background
Flash flooding can strike with little warning and quickly overwhelm roads, homes, businesses, and public transportation systems. When water rises fast, drivers can become trapped, train and metro services can grind to a halt, and emergency responders may struggle to reach people in time.
Extreme weather disasters put lives and livelihoods at risk by disrupting work, damaging property, and threatening public health. Floodwater can carry debris, sewage, and other contaminants, while washed-out roads and suspended transit can delay medical care, isolate neighborhoods, and interrupt paychecks for workers who cannot safely travel.
Scenes from eastern Spain also demonstrated how vulnerable urban infrastructure can be during intense rainfall. A flooded metro station can bring commuter delays, cleanup costs, and safety risks that continue even after the rain has stopped.
What's being done?
The immediate response centered on warnings, travel guidance, and rescue operations. AEMET's red alert for Barcelona's coastline and authorities' advice against unnecessary travel were intended to reduce preventable emergencies while crews dealt with the most dangerous conditions.
Staying off the roads during flash floods can save lives and reduce strain on first responders. Flooded streets may be deeper or faster-moving than they appear, and low-lying areas such as tunnels, underpasses, and transit entrances can become dangerous within minutes.
